Next I’ll pull location details and current fire-weather data for that area.Pulling live fire detections, weather, and site layout next so the risk call is checkable.**Elevated for mid-monsoon, not peak dry-season risk.** At Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) near Chinnathamandrapalli / Veppanapalli (Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu), I would call current fire danger **moderate–high for July**, driven by a weak monsoon, recent heat, and very little recent rain—not the classic Jan–May peak, but meaningfully dry for this date. **Highest risk is the forest–village edge and the steeper NE/E hillslopes**; put a small set of patrols/sensors on that edge, an upslope lookout, and the campus/nursery.

---

### Where and what EBTL is
EBTL is a ~68–70 acre dry-deciduous restoration site in a valley between forest and **Chinnathamandrapalli (CT Palli)** near Veppanapalli, Krishnagiri—denuded land with an old elephant walkway and waterhole, surrounded by Eastern Ghats hills ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/); [Biosmart / Rainmatter description](https://portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2); village coords ≈ **12.728°N, 78.174°E**, ~724 m).

---

### Current fire risk (as of 20 Jul 2026)

| Factor | Finding | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Active fires (24h) | NASA FIRMS South Asia 24h VIIRS/MODIS: **0** detections in 12.4–13.1°N, 77.8–78.5°E | No ongoing blaze on/near site today |
| Recent fires (7d) | NOAA-20 VIIRS: detection **~3 km SE** of CT Palli on **15 Jul** (12.716°N, 78.194°E, night, FRP ~2.3 MW, nominal). Others ~30–60 km W toward Hosur/Bengaluru fringe | Ignition is happening in the neighbourhood; treat as local human/agri/industrial heat until ground-truthed |
| Weather now | Open-Meteo at site: ~25°C, RH ~67%, wind ~13 km/h W, no precip at observation time | Night-time safer; daytime dries fast |
| Rain / drought | Archive: **Jan–May 2026 precip ~65 mm**; **June ~80 mm**; **1–19 Jul only ~11 mm** with **15/19 days <1 mm**. Surface soil moisture ~0.10–0.11 m³/m³ | Fuels not as cured as April, but understory grass/litter can still carry fire after multi-day dry spells |
| Regional climate | RMC/The Hindu (16 Jul): weak SW monsoon + El Niño–linked heat over interior TN through ~17 Jul; southern peninsula rainfall ~35% below LPA early July ([The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/abnormal-heatwave-conditions-to-persist-across-tamil-nadu-till-july-17-rainfall-set-to-improve-later-this-week/article71226160.ece); [BusinessLine](https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/fractured-monsoon-july-recovery-narrows-overall-deficit-to-23-but-key-regions-remain-dry/article71224862.ece)) | July risk is **anomalously high** for monsoon |
| Seasonality | TN / Eastern Ghats fire season typically **Jan–May** (often into early monsoon on cumulative drought); >90–95% fires human-caused ([NDRF forest fire brief](https://www.ndrf.gov.in/sites/default/files/Forset%20Fire.pdf); Vellore WDI study: dry May–Jul fuel pressure ([Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/remote-sensing/articles/10.3389/frsen.2025.1518539/full))) | Peak risk still ahead (post-NE monsoon into next dry season), but prep now is right |

**Verdict now:** **Moderate–High (elevated off-season)**. Not “extreme dry-season” yet, but dry enough that an escaped burn or spark at the village–forest edge could run into scrub/grass and upslope into remnant forest and young restoration plantings. 2026 nationally is already a severe fire year early on ([Down To Earth](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/why-2026-stands-out-as-a-worrying-year-for-forest-fires-in-india)).

Crude daytime danger from Open-Meteo (hot + low RH + little rain + wind): several recent/forecast days score **High–Extreme** on that proxy (esp. 11–16 Jul and again ~23–24 Jul)—use as weather stress, not a full FWI.

---

### Where risk is highest on/near the property

Without a published parcel map, this is based on site description + SRTM30 topography around CT Palli:

1. **Forest–village interface (highest priority)** — EBTL sits between CT Palli and degraded forest; India-wide, fringe ignition (grazing, litter burns, NTFP, cooking, cigarettes, intentional clearing) dominates ([NDRF](https://www.ndrf.gov.in/sites/default/files/Forset%20Fire.pdf)). Melagiri/Eastern Ghats threats explicitly include fire and biotic pressure ([Wikipedia Melagiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melagiri)).
2. **Steep NE / E hillslopes** — SRTM around the village: valley ~560–580 m; hills to the **N/NE/E rise to ~840 m** within ~2 km, with local slopes >0.25–0.35 rise/run. Fire runs **upslope**; ridges also get more wind and faster fine-fuel curing.
3. **Denuded grass/scrub and young restoration patches** — fine fuels cure first; continuous grass on undulating land is the classic dry-deciduous carry fuel (cf. Theni “manjapul” dry grass narrative).
4. **Elephant walkway / waterhole approaches** — human and livestock paths concentrate ignition risk and complicate evacuation of people/animals.
5. **Lower absolute risk today:** irrigated farm plots and the wettest waterhole margin (still protect as assets/refugia).

OSM nearby: scrub ~S of Veppanapalli, wood farther NW, a waterbody ~WNW of CT Palli—consistent with a mosaic of farm, scrub, and remnant woody cover.

---

### Where to put a **small** number of patrols / sensors (before dry season)

Assume **3–5** nodes. Prefer **human-path + upslope early-warning** over uniform grid.

| Priority | Location | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Main tracks from CT Palli into EBTL / forest edge (esp. SE–E toward the 15 Jul hotspot bearing) | Catch escaped burns; community liaison with Chinnathamandrapalli |
| **2** | Mid–upper NE/E slope or ridge overlooking the valley | Detect upslope runs; wind-exposed early smoke |
| **3** | Campus / nursery / farm–restoration boundary | Asset protection; staff response hub |
| **4** (if 4th) | Elephant walkway / waterhole approach | Path ignition + wildlife safety |
| **5** (if 5th) | Opposite scrub edge with continuous fine fuel into plantings | Spot secondary spread |

**Ops notes:** Pair sensors (smoke/thermal camera or simple LoRa temp–RH + camera) with **scheduled foot patrols at the village edge in late morning–afternoon** on dry, windy days; clear 5–10 m fuel breaks around nursery/structures; agree with village on **no open burning** Nov–May and during multi-day dry spells in monsoon. Subscribe to [FSI Van Agni / fire alerts](https://fsiforestfire.gov.in/) for Krishnagiri.

---

### Method (so you can check)

1. **Place:** EBTL = Rainmatter restoration at CT Palli / Veppanapalli ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/), [portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2](https://portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2)); village lat/lon from public gazetteer (~12.727, 78.174).
2. **Active fire:** NASA FIRMS public CSVs (`J1_VIIRS_C2_South_Asia_{24h,7d}.csv`, Suomi VIIRS, MODIS) filtered to a Krishnagiri box; nearest 7d hit ~3 km SE on 15 Jul 2026.
3. **Weather/fuel:** Open-Meteo forecast + ERA5-Land archive for precip, RH, wind, soil moisture, ET0 at 12.727°N, 78.174°E (queried 20 Jul 2026).
4. **Terrain:** OpenTopoData SRTM30m grid ±~2 km for elevation/slope proxies.
5. **Context:** RMC heat/monsoon reporting; IMD/monsoon deficit reporting; NDRF/FSI fire-season and cause literature; 2026 national fire surge (DTE/FIRMS).

**Limits:** Exact EBTL cadastral boundary and internal fuel map were not public; the 15 Jul VIIRS point is **not** confirmed forest fire (could be agri/industrial); full Canadian FWI was not available from Open-Meteo here—danger is a transparent weather proxy plus season/fuel reasoning. For a tighter map, overlay your polygon on FSI alerts + a 10 m fuel/NDVI layer and walk the NE slopes once before Nov.

**Bottom line:** Treat EBTL as **elevated risk now** because July is abnormally dry/hot; **concentrate scarce patrols/sensors on the CT Palli–forest edge and the steep NE/E hills**, then harden the nursery/campus before the main dry season.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) - A forest restoration project in the Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu

Over decades, the dry deciduous forests of our country have been stripped and exploited for commercial use. As native forests receded to only higher elevations of hills, creatures of the forests have also lost their footing in the valley. EBTL lies in one of those valleys. In the foothills of a degraded forest.

These 70 acres now 'belong' to us. How wonderful would it be if the other creatures also echoed the same thought? Our goal is to help the forest regain its rich biodiversity.

The year we began work, a few elephants came to the land, something that had never happened in the last many decades. We decided to call this project.

# Elephants By The Lake!

# The map of EBTL

Once you step into the hills around EBTL there are remnants of a once thriving forest; bird calls, fresh bear tracks, the jumping away of a troupe of langurs, trees in bloom or seed, spiders waiting for a catch, the scuffling across of a monitor lizard, a bird of prey gliding above.

Unfortunately this biodiverse ecosystem of the Eastern Ghats has been almost eradicated in terms of its area, but for a few hilly pockets where the tough terrain has made it too difficult for people to interfere.

Hopefully in time, the land will begin a cycle of regeneration where at a point, this space can become a safe corner for some of the rarer and threatened flora of the Eastern Ghats to flourish and wildlife can reinhabit the land.

# What happens at EBTL

#### Forest restoration

EBTL, primarily is focused on the native flora of the dry decidious forests of the South Deccan plateau.

#### Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies

We have established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

#### Organic farming

A small percentage of land we own is allotted for farming where we grow paddy, pulses, millets and vegetables.

#### Farmer's Collective

We work very closely with the nearby village of Chinnathamandrapalli. The villagers play a vital role in all the work we undertake. We have enabled a collective of women working towards value added products. They also manage our farm lands and campus.

# Farmer's Collective

We promote land stewardship and sustainable farming by employing the local community and supporting a farmers collective to create value-added products. Our goal is to provide eco-friendly job opportunities to counter urban migration among the younger generation.

<content># Drop Down Sections for Elephants:
...
If elephants are present in the area, “drop down” fence sections will be needed. Elephants cannot crawl under or jump over any fence, and unless given an opening, will create one by taking down the fence.
...
As the name suggests, these sections of the fence can be dropped or removed when needed. Carefully placed drop down fence sections allow us to create safe corridors for the elephants to pass through our property, while reducing the likelihood of their taking down the fence elsewhere in order to get in. After the animals have moved on from the area, the fence can be brought back up to close the openings.
...
The drop down section (dark) is secured to the fence (light) using wire loops near the top and the base of the staffs.
...
The Base loop is permanently secured around the standard fence pole (light).
...
To erect the drop down section (dark), it is placed base first into the base loop, with both poles parallel.
...
The top loop is then flung over the two poles and is used to secure them.
...
To “drop” the section, the process is reversed. [1. Remove the top loop > 2. Pull out the drop down section > 3. Welcome the elephants in]
...
A drop down section. Wire types (barbed/smooth) and the gaps between them are the same as other sections. This section isn’t fixed to the ground. Two constraint staffs are provided to maintain wire gaps, which would otherwise be subject to distortion when the section is moved.</content>

# In-House Research at EBTL

The Eastern Ghats are among the oldest mountain systems on Earth, with geological origins tracing back to the Precambrian era. Yet, despite their age and ecological significance, the Eastern Ghats remain one of India’s least studied landscapes, especially when compared to the Western Ghats.

Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) has established a dedicated in-house field research initiative at our campus in Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu, to address critical gaps in knowledge about Eastern Ghats biodiversity, ecology, and conservation priorities.

Our work begins with intensive field-based studies on herpetofauna and arachnids, groups that act as sensitive indicators of ecosystem health. EBTL’s research integrates multiple scientific disciplines, including:

# Why 2026 stands out as a worrying year for forest fires in India

DTE analysis shows wildfires growing more frequent and intense, with forest fires in India up over 80% in early 2026 compared to the past decade

iStock

Pulaha Roy

Published on:

Copied

Summary

Forest fires in India have risen by over 80% in early 2026 compared with the past decade

Fire activity is more than 50% higher than in 2024, the warmest year on record

Intensity of fires has also increased, with more severe and energy-intensive burns reported

North-east India remains the worst affected, but spikes are seen across Himalayan states, Odisha and southern regions

Fires are starting earlier in the season, raising concerns about climate-linked risks

When it comes to forest fires, 2026 is emerging as a concerning outlier. Early data suggests that both the number of fires and their intensity have risen sharply, pointing to a potentially severe fire season.

An analysis of fire activity by Down To Earth (DTE) indicated that forest fires in the first two months of 2026 increased by more than 80 per cent compared with trends over the past decade since 2014. When compared with the warmest year on record 2024, fire activity in forested regions was over 50 per cent higher.

However, it is not only the number of fires that is worrying. The intensity of these fires, measured by the rate of thermal energy released by burning vegetation, has also increased compared with previous years.

North East India has consistently reported some of the most intense forest fires, and this trend continues. But the increase is not limited to that region. Spikes in fire intensity have also been recorded in the Himalayan states of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, in Odisha in the east, and in the Rayalaseema region in southern India.

To assess fire trends, DTE mapped forest regions using OpenStreetMap data and overlaid fire activity data from National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) S-NPP system.

NASA FIRMS defines fire intensity primarily through fire radiative power, which measures the rate of emitted radiative energy (in megawatts) from a fire, typically derived from satellite thermal sensors.

The data was filtered to include only fire points within forested areas and analysed based on fire intensity.

### Early and expanding fire season

Forest fires have also begun earlier than usual this year. In Uttarakhand, fires swept through hill regions unusually early in the season. Between November 1, 2025 and February 14, 2026, the state forest department recorded 54 fire incidents, affecting around 42 hectares of forest — roughly the size of 60 football pitches.

As temperatures continued to rise, another 60 fires were reported between February 15 and March 14, affecting a similar area. Residents have also reported prolonged fire activity. Forests near Naurakh village were covered in smoke during winter, with local resident Reena Devi saying nearby forests burned for several days in January.

North East India has seen particularly severe outbreaks. In February, large swathes of Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland were engulfed for a week, prompting sustained aerial firefighting by the Indian Air Force (IAF) in high-altitude Himalayan terrain. Helicopters were deployed to spray water at elevations above 2,800 metres. In the Lohit valley of Arunachal Pradesh, over 12,000 litres of water were dropped to contain the flames.

The fires in the state reportedly began on February 13, affected multiple areas and prompted evacuations in some localities. Local media reported that Indian Army personnel joined IAF teams to tackle fires in remote parts of Anjaw district, at altitudes of 900 to 1,060 metres.

Women shield themselves from the scorching sun with umbrellas in Chennai. File. | Photo Credit: The Hindu

The weak Southwest monsoon circulation, along with El Niño-induced subsidence, is expected to sustain abnormal heatwave conditions over interior Tamil Nadu till Friday (July 17, 2026). The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) has forecast an improvement in rainfall over the State from the second half of the week and ease the prevailing heatwave conditions.

On Wednesday, many places, particularly interior parts of Tamil Nadu, continued to sizzle as the mercury level climbed above 40 degree Celsius. While the mercury levels hit 41.6 degrees Celsius in Vellore, the highest in the State for the day, places like Madurai and Tiruttani too witnessed temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius.

Chennai sweltered under searing heat on Wednesday, as Nungambakkam recorded a maximum temperature of 39.4 degrees Celsius, the highest for July in the city since 2019. The weather station had previously registered a maximum temperature of 40.4 degrees Celsius on July 5, 2019.

Meenambakkam too recorded a high day temperature of 40.1 degrees Celsius as strong South-westerlies and dry weather prevailed. The city may have to brace for another hot day, as the maximum temperature is likely to hover around 38-39 degrees Celsius on Thursday.

Officials of the RMC said the weak monsoon circulation over the Southern Peninsular region and El Niño-related atmospheric conditions led to limited cloud formation and an unusual heat spell in July. The RMC has issued a heatwave warning for isolated places in 19 interior and northern districts, including Vellore, Kancheepuram, Erode, Salem and Madurai, on Thursday, as day temperatures may soar two to four degrees Celsius above normal. Seven districts, including Namakkal, Karur and Madurai, are likely to experience heatwave conditions on Friday. Coastal areas of the State are likely to experience hot and humid weather till Friday.

V.R. Durai, Head, Regional Weather Forecasting Centre, RMC, said the weak Somali Jet, a low-level wind stream that transports moisture from the Arabian Sea, is likely to strengthen gradually from Friday and revive monsoon conditions over the Southern Peninsular region.

A weather system likely over the northwest Bay of Bengal would also support monsoon revival. Though the revival may be a weak one, it would still improve cloud cover and rainfall in the State from Friday and help keep temperatures in check.

While Madurai has experienced soaring July temperatures, various other places experienced unusual heatwave conditions spread over three to four days, he added.

**Elevated for mid-monsoon, not peak dry-season risk.** At Elephants By The Lake (EBTL) near Chinnathamandrapalli / Veppanapalli (Krishnagiri, Tamil Nadu), I would call current fire danger **moderate–high for July**, driven by a weak monsoon, recent heat, and very little recent rain—not the classic Jan–May peak, but meaningfully dry for this date. **Highest risk is the forest–village edge and the steeper NE/E hillslopes**; put a small set of patrols/sensors on that edge, an upslope lookout, and the campus/nursery.

---

### Where and what EBTL is
EBTL is a ~68–70 acre dry-deciduous restoration site in a valley between forest and **Chinnathamandrapalli (CT Palli)** near Veppanapalli, Krishnagiri—denuded land with an old elephant walkway and waterhole, surrounded by Eastern Ghats hills ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/); [Biosmart / Rainmatter description](https://portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2); village coords ≈ **12.728°N, 78.174°E**, ~724 m).

---

### Current fire risk (as of 20 Jul 2026)

| Factor | Finding | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Active fires (24h) | NASA FIRMS South Asia 24h VIIRS/MODIS: **0** detections in 12.4–13.1°N, 77.8–78.5°E | No ongoing blaze on/near site today |
| Recent fires (7d) | NOAA-20 VIIRS: detection **~3 km SE** of CT Palli on **15 Jul** (12.716°N, 78.194°E, night, FRP ~2.3 MW, nominal). Others ~30–60 km W toward Hosur/Bengaluru fringe | Ignition is happening in the neighbourhood; treat as local human/agri/industrial heat until ground-truthed |
| Weather now | Open-Meteo at site: ~25°C, RH ~67%, wind ~13 km/h W, no precip at observation time | Night-time safer; daytime dries fast |
| Rain / drought | Archive: **Jan–May 2026 precip ~65 mm**; **June ~80 mm**; **1–19 Jul only ~11 mm** with **15/19 days <1 mm**. Surface soil moisture ~0.10–0.11 m³/m³ | Fuels not as cured as April, but understory grass/litter can still carry fire after multi-day dry spells |
| Regional climate | RMC/The Hindu (16 Jul): weak SW monsoon + El Niño–linked heat over interior TN through ~17 Jul; southern peninsula rainfall ~35% below LPA early July ([The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/tamil-nadu/abnormal-heatwave-conditions-to-persist-across-tamil-nadu-till-july-17-rainfall-set-to-improve-later-this-week/article71226160.ece); [BusinessLine](https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/economy/fractured-monsoon-july-recovery-narrows-overall-deficit-to-23-but-key-regions-remain-dry/article71224862.ece)) | July risk is **anomalously high** for monsoon |
| Seasonality | TN / Eastern Ghats fire season typically **Jan–May** (often into early monsoon on cumulative drought); >90–95% fires human-caused ([NDRF forest fire brief](https://www.ndrf.gov.in/sites/default/files/Forset%20Fire.pdf); Vellore WDI study: dry May–Jul fuel pressure ([Frontiers](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/remote-sensing/articles/10.3389/frsen.2025.1518539/full))) | Peak risk still ahead (post-NE monsoon into next dry season), but prep now is right |

**Verdict now:** **Moderate–High (elevated off-season)**. Not “extreme dry-season” yet, but dry enough that an escaped burn or spark at the village–forest edge could run into scrub/grass and upslope into remnant forest and young restoration plantings. 2026 nationally is already a severe fire year early on ([Down To Earth](https://www.downtoearth.org.in/climate-change/why-2026-stands-out-as-a-worrying-year-for-forest-fires-in-india)).

Crude daytime danger from Open-Meteo (hot + low RH + little rain + wind): several recent/forecast days score **High–Extreme** on that proxy (esp. 11–16 Jul and again ~23–24 Jul)—use as weather stress, not a full FWI.

---

### Where risk is highest on/near the property

Without a published parcel map, this is based on site description + SRTM30 topography around CT Palli:

1. **Forest–village interface (highest priority)** — EBTL sits between CT Palli and degraded forest; India-wide, fringe ignition (grazing, litter burns, NTFP, cooking, cigarettes, intentional clearing) dominates ([NDRF](https://www.ndrf.gov.in/sites/default/files/Forset%20Fire.pdf)). Melagiri/Eastern Ghats threats explicitly include fire and biotic pressure ([Wikipedia Melagiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melagiri)).
2. **Steep NE / E hillslopes** — SRTM around the village: valley ~560–580 m; hills to the **N/NE/E rise to ~840 m** within ~2 km, with local slopes >0.25–0.35 rise/run. Fire runs **upslope**; ridges also get more wind and faster fine-fuel curing.
3. **Denuded grass/scrub and young restoration patches** — fine fuels cure first; continuous grass on undulating land is the classic dry-deciduous carry fuel (cf. Theni “manjapul” dry grass narrative).
4. **Elephant walkway / waterhole approaches** — human and livestock paths concentrate ignition risk and complicate evacuation of people/animals.
5. **Lower absolute risk today:** irrigated farm plots and the wettest waterhole margin (still protect as assets/refugia).

OSM nearby: scrub ~S of Veppanapalli, wood farther NW, a waterbody ~WNW of CT Palli—consistent with a mosaic of farm, scrub, and remnant woody cover.

---

### Where to put a **small** number of patrols / sensors (before dry season)

Assume **3–5** nodes. Prefer **human-path + upslope early-warning** over uniform grid.

| Priority | Location | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Main tracks from CT Palli into EBTL / forest edge (esp. SE–E toward the 15 Jul hotspot bearing) | Catch escaped burns; community liaison with Chinnathamandrapalli |
| **2** | Mid–upper NE/E slope or ridge overlooking the valley | Detect upslope runs; wind-exposed early smoke |
| **3** | Campus / nursery / farm–restoration boundary | Asset protection; staff response hub |
| **4** (if 4th) | Elephant walkway / waterhole approach | Path ignition + wildlife safety |
| **5** (if 5th) | Opposite scrub edge with continuous fine fuel into plantings | Spot secondary spread |

**Ops notes:** Pair sensors (smoke/thermal camera or simple LoRa temp–RH + camera) with **scheduled foot patrols at the village edge in late morning–afternoon** on dry, windy days; clear 5–10 m fuel breaks around nursery/structures; agree with village on **no open burning** Nov–May and during multi-day dry spells in monsoon. Subscribe to [FSI Van Agni / fire alerts](https://fsiforestfire.gov.in/) for Krishnagiri.

---

### Method (so you can check)

1. **Place:** EBTL = Rainmatter restoration at CT Palli / Veppanapalli ([ebtl.earth](https://ebtl.earth/), [portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2](https://portal.biosmart.life/ebtl2)); village lat/lon from public gazetteer (~12.727, 78.174).
2. **Active fire:** NASA FIRMS public CSVs (`J1_VIIRS_C2_South_Asia_{24h,7d}.csv`, Suomi VIIRS, MODIS) filtered to a Krishnagiri box; nearest 7d hit ~3 km SE on 15 Jul 2026.
3. **Weather/fuel:** Open-Meteo forecast + ERA5-Land archive for precip, RH, wind, soil moisture, ET0 at 12.727°N, 78.174°E (queried 20 Jul 2026).
4. **Terrain:** OpenTopoData SRTM30m grid ±~2 km for elevation/slope proxies.
5. **Context:** RMC heat/monsoon reporting; IMD/monsoon deficit reporting; NDRF/FSI fire-season and cause literature; 2026 national fire surge (DTE/FIRMS).

**Limits:** Exact EBTL cadastral boundary and internal fuel map were not public; the 15 Jul VIIRS point is **not** confirmed forest fire (could be agri/industrial); full Canadian FWI was not available from Open-Meteo here—danger is a transparent weather proxy plus season/fuel reasoning. For a tighter map, overlay your polygon on FSI alerts + a 10 m fuel/NDVI layer and walk the NE slopes once before Nov.

**Bottom line:** Treat EBTL as **elevated risk now** because July is abnormally dry/hot; **concentrate scarce patrols/sensors on the CT Palli–forest edge and the steep NE/E hills**, then harden the nursery/campus before the main dry season.

### Where risk is highest on/near the property

Without a published parcel map, this is based on site description + SRTM30 topography around CT Palli:

1. **Forest–village interface (highest priority)** — EBTL sits between CT Palli and degraded forest; India-wide, fringe ignition (grazing, litter burns, NTFP, cooking, cigarettes, intentional clearing) dominates ([NDRF](https://www.ndrf.gov.in/sites/default/files/Forset%20Fire.pdf)). Melagiri/Eastern Ghats threats explicitly include fire and biotic pressure ([Wikipedia Melagiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melagiri)).
2. **Steep NE / E hillslopes** — SRTM around the village: valley ~560–580 m; hills to the **N/NE/E rise to ~840 m** within ~2 km, with local slopes >0.25–0.35 rise/run. Fire runs **upslope**; ridges also get more wind and faster fine-fuel curing.
3. **Denuded grass/scrub and young restoration patches** — fine fuels cure first; continuous grass on undulating land is the classic dry-deciduous carry fuel (cf. Theni “manjapul” dry grass narrative).
4. **Elephant walkway / waterhole approaches** — human and livestock paths concentrate ignition risk and complicate evacuation of people/animals.
5. **Lower absolute risk today:** irrigated farm plots and the wettest waterhole margin (still protect as assets/refugia).

OSM nearby: scrub ~S of Veppanapalli, wood farther NW, a waterbody ~WNW of CT Palli—consistent with a mosaic of farm, scrub, and remnant woody cover.

5. **Context:** RMC heat/monsoon reporting; IMD/monsoon deficit reporting; NDRF/FSI fire-season and cause literature; 2026 national fire surge (DTE/FIRMS).

**Bottom line:** Treat EBTL as **elevated risk now** because July is abnormally dry/hot; **concentrate scarce patrols/sensors on the CT Palli–forest edge and the steep NE/E hills**, then harden the nursery/campus before the main dry season.
